subject: grade-10-physical-sciences
description: Grade 10 Physical Sciences skill tree (CAPS FET). 18 levels (one per CAPS topic) split across Physics (P1) and Chemistry (P2), covering the six CAPS knowledge areas: Mechanics, Waves/Sound/Light, Electricity & Magnetism, Matter & Materials, Chemical Change, Chemical Systems. 27 atomic skills. Tap-native bank (choice / numeric / sequence — no free-text). Items live in data/grade-10-physical-sciences-question-banks/<skill-id>.json.

levels.title: Motion in One Dimension
levels.description: Reference frames, position, distance vs displacement, speed vs velocity, acceleration; equations of motion for uniform acceleration; motion graphs.

atomic_skills.title: Distinguish distance/displacement and speed/velocity; describe motion
atomic_skills.description: Define and distinguish reference frame, position, distance (scalar, path length) vs displacement (vector, straight-line change in position), speed (scalar) vs velocity (vector), and acceleration. Identify which quantity is a vector and which is a scalar, and read off magnitude and direction.

error_signatures.description: Treats distance and displacement as the same quantity
error_signatures.example: Says a runner who completes one lap of a 400 m track has a displacement of 400 m

error_signatures.description: Calls velocity a scalar / drops the direction
error_signatures.example: Gives velocity as 5 m/s with no direction stated

error_signatures.description: Confuses speed and velocity definitions
error_signatures.example: Defines speed as rate of change of displacement

error_signatures.description: Reports a negative displacement as a distance
error_signatures.example: Records a displacement of -3 m as a distance of -3 m

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Distance and speed are SCALARS (size only). Displacement and velocity are VECTORS (size AND direction). Distance = total path travelled; displacement = straight line from start to end with direction. Speed = distance/time; velocity = displacement/time. Always state a direction for a vector.

atomic_skills.title: Apply the equations of motion for uniform acceleration
atomic_skills.description: Use v = u + at, Δx = uΔt + ½aΔt², v² = u² + 2aΔx, Δx = ½(u+v)Δt to solve one-dimensional motion problems with constant acceleration (including free fall, g = 9.8 m·s⁻²).

error_signatures.description: Picks an equation that needs a quantity not given
error_signatures.example: Uses v = u + at when t is unknown and not asked for

error_signatures.description: Uses inconsistent signs for direction
error_signatures.example: Takes upward as positive but substitutes a = +9.8 m/s² for a falling object

error_signatures.description: Forgets initial velocity is zero only when stated
error_signatures.example: Sets u = 0 for an object that was already moving

error_signatures.description: Mixes up Δx and v in v² = u² + 2aΔx
error_signatures.example: Solves for displacement but reports it as velocity

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Choose a positive direction and keep all signs consistent. List u, v, a, Δx, Δt — you know three, pick the equation linking your three knowns to the unknown. Free fall: a = g downward. Released from rest ⇒ u = 0; 'dropped' ⇒ u = 0.

atomic_skills.title: Interpret and sketch position-time, velocity-time and acceleration-time graphs
atomic_skills.description: Read displacement, velocity and acceleration off motion graphs; relate gradient and area between graph types (gradient of x-t = velocity; gradient of v-t = acceleration; area under v-t = displacement); match a described motion to the correct graph.

error_signatures.description: Reads the value on a v-t graph as displacement instead of using the area
error_signatures.example: Says displacement equals the velocity reading at that instant

error_signatures.description: Confuses the gradient of x-t with the gradient of v-t
error_signatures.example: Calls the slope of a position-time graph the acceleration

error_signatures.description: Ignores that velocity below the time axis means motion in the negative direction
error_signatures.example: Reports a -2 m/s reading as motion in the positive direction

error_signatures.description: Says a horizontal line on a v-t graph means the object is stationary
error_signatures.example: Reads constant non-zero velocity as 'at rest'

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: x-t graph: gradient = velocity. v-t graph: gradient = acceleration, AREA underneath = displacement. A flat x-t line = at rest; a flat non-zero v-t line = constant velocity. A line crossing below the axis = motion reversed direction.

levels.title: Energy
levels.description: Gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, mechanical energy and the conservation of mechanical energy.

atomic_skills.title: Calculate gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy
atomic_skills.description: Define and calculate gravitational potential energy (Ep = mgh) and kinetic energy (Ek = ½mv²); identify how each changes as height or speed changes.

error_signatures.description: Uses ½mv instead of ½mv² for kinetic energy
error_signatures.example: Writes Ek = ½mv

error_signatures.description: Doubles speed and predicts kinetic energy doubles
error_signatures.example: Says Ek doubles when v doubles instead of quadrupling

error_signatures.description: Uses the wrong height reference for potential energy
error_signatures.example: Measures h from the top instead of the chosen zero level

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Ep = mgh (h above a chosen zero level). Ek = ½mv² — speed is SQUARED, so doubling v makes Ek four times bigger. Always state where h = 0 is and measure heights from there.

atomic_skills.title: Apply conservation of mechanical energy
atomic_skills.description: Define mechanical energy (Em = Ep + Ek); apply the principle of conservation of mechanical energy (in the absence of friction/air resistance) to find speed or height at points in free fall, on inclines, or for falling/rising objects.

error_signatures.description: Applies conservation of mechanical energy when friction is present
error_signatures.example: Uses Em(top) = Em(bottom) on a rough slope

error_signatures.description: Forgets that total mechanical energy stays constant, not Ep or Ek alone
error_signatures.example: Sets Ep at the top equal to Ek at the bottom but adds the wrong terms

error_signatures.description: Thinks a heavier object reaches the ground with a higher speed in free fall
error_signatures.example: Predicts a 2 kg ball lands faster than a 1 kg ball dropped from the same height

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Mechanical energy Em = Ep + Ek. With no friction, Em is conserved: (Ep + Ek) at the start = (Ep + Ek) at the end. As an object falls, Ep converts to Ek but the TOTAL stays the same. Mass cancels in free fall, so final speed is independent of mass.

levels.title: Transverse Pulses and Waves
levels.description: Transverse pulses on a string/spring, superposition; transverse waves — amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, wave speed.

atomic_skills.title: Describe transverse pulses and superposition
atomic_skills.description: Define a pulse and a transverse pulse; identify amplitude and pulse length; apply the principle of superposition to find the resultant when two pulses meet (constructive and destructive interference).

error_signatures.description: Adds pulse lengths instead of amplitudes during superposition
error_signatures.example: Says two overlapping pulses combine their widths

error_signatures.description: Says pulses are destroyed permanently after destructive interference
error_signatures.example: Claims two pulses cancel and never reappear

error_signatures.description: Confuses amplitude with wavelength for a pulse
error_signatures.example: Calls the horizontal length of a pulse its amplitude

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: A pulse is a single disturbance; transverse means the medium moves perpendicular to the pulse's travel. Superposition: when pulses overlap, ADD their displacements (amplitudes). Same side ⇒ constructive (bigger); opposite sides ⇒ destructive (cancel). After overlapping they pass through and continue unchanged.

atomic_skills.title: Relate wavelength, frequency, period and wave speed for transverse waves
atomic_skills.description: Define amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period and crest/trough for a transverse wave; apply T = 1/f and v = fλ to calculate any one quantity from the others.

error_signatures.description: Confuses period and frequency (uses f where T belongs)
error_signatures.example: Substitutes frequency into v = fλ as if it were the period

error_signatures.description: Measures wavelength crest-to-trough instead of crest-to-crest
error_signatures.example: Calls the distance from a crest to the next trough one wavelength

error_signatures.description: Forgets T = 1/f when only the period is given
error_signatures.example: Puts the period straight into v = fλ

error_signatures.description: Thinks amplitude affects wave speed or wavelength
error_signatures.example: Says a bigger amplitude makes the wave travel faster

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Wavelength λ = distance for ONE full wave (crest-to-crest or trough-to-trough). Period T = time for one wave; frequency f = waves per second; T = 1/f. Wave speed v = fλ. Amplitude (height) is independent of speed and wavelength.

levels.title: Longitudinal Waves and Sound
levels.description: Longitudinal waves (compressions and rarefactions); sound as a longitudinal wave — pitch, loudness, quality, speed of sound, echoes and ultrasound.

atomic_skills.title: Describe longitudinal waves and apply v = fλ
atomic_skills.description: Define a longitudinal wave; identify compressions and rarefactions, wavelength, frequency and amplitude; contrast transverse and longitudinal waves; apply v = fλ to longitudinal (including sound) waves.

error_signatures.description: Says particles in a longitudinal wave move perpendicular to wave travel
error_signatures.example: Describes sound particles vibrating at right angles to the direction the sound travels

error_signatures.description: Confuses compression and rarefaction
error_signatures.example: Calls the low-pressure region a compression

error_signatures.description: Measures wavelength compression-to-rarefaction
error_signatures.example: Calls the gap from a compression to the next rarefaction one wavelength

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Longitudinal: particles vibrate PARALLEL to the wave's travel (back and forth). Compression = particles bunched (high pressure); rarefaction = particles spread out (low pressure). Wavelength = compression-to-compression. v = fλ still applies.

atomic_skills.title: Relate properties of sound to pitch, loudness and quality
atomic_skills.description: Relate frequency to pitch, amplitude to loudness, and waveform to quality (tone); describe the speed of sound in different media; apply sound concepts to echoes, ultrasound and sonar.

error_signatures.description: Swaps pitch and loudness with their wave properties
error_signatures.example: Says a higher amplitude raises the pitch

error_signatures.description: Thinks sound travels fastest in a gas
error_signatures.example: Says sound is faster in air than in steel

error_signatures.description: Says sound can travel through a vacuum
error_signatures.example: Claims sound from a bell is heard inside an evacuated jar

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Pitch ↔ frequency (high f = high pitch). Loudness ↔ amplitude (big amplitude = loud). Quality/tone ↔ waveform shape. Sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases, and CANNOT travel through a vacuum (it needs a medium). Ultrasound = frequency above 20 000 Hz.

levels.title: Electromagnetic Radiation
levels.description: The electromagnetic spectrum, the relationship between frequency, wavelength and energy, the dual (wave/particle) nature of EM radiation, uses and dangers of each band.

atomic_skills.title: Describe the EM spectrum and relate frequency, wavelength and energy
atomic_skills.description: List the bands of the EM spectrum in order; apply c = fλ and E = hf; relate higher frequency to shorter wavelength and higher photon energy; state uses and dangers of each band and describe the dual nature of EM radiation.

error_signatures.description: Orders the EM spectrum incorrectly
error_signatures.example: Places ultraviolet between radio waves and microwaves

error_signatures.description: Says longer wavelength means higher energy
error_signatures.example: Claims radio waves carry more energy than gamma rays

error_signatures.description: Uses wavelength instead of frequency in E = hf
error_signatures.example: Substitutes λ for f when finding photon energy

error_signatures.description: Thinks different EM bands travel at different speeds in a vacuum
error_signatures.example: Says X-rays travel faster than visible light in a vacuum

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Order (low to high frequency): radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma. All travel at c = 3×10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. c = fλ, so higher f ⇒ shorter λ. E = hf, so higher f ⇒ higher energy. Gamma = highest energy/most dangerous; radio = lowest.

levels.title: Magnetism
levels.description: Magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion, magnetic fields and field lines, the Earth's magnetic field and the compass.

atomic_skills.title: Describe magnetic fields, poles and the Earth's magnetic field
atomic_skills.description: State the rule for attraction/repulsion of magnetic poles; draw and interpret magnetic field lines around a bar magnet (direction N→S outside the magnet, never crossing); describe the Earth's magnetic field and how a compass works.

error_signatures.description: Says like poles attract
error_signatures.example: Predicts two north poles pull together

error_signatures.description: Draws field lines from S to N outside the magnet
error_signatures.example: Shows field arrows pointing into the north pole outside the magnet

error_signatures.description: Says magnetic field lines can cross
error_signatures.example: Draws two field lines intersecting between two magnets

error_signatures.description: Confuses the Earth's geographic and magnetic poles
error_signatures.example: Says a compass needle's north points to the Earth's magnetic north pole

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract. Field lines run from N to S OUTSIDE the magnet, are closer together where the field is stronger, and never cross. The Earth acts like a bar magnet with its magnetic SOUTH near the geographic north, which is why a compass north needle points geographically north.

levels.title: Electrostatics
levels.description: Two kinds of charge, charging objects, conservation and quantisation of charge, force between charges (qualitative), Q = ne calculations.

atomic_skills.title: Apply charge concepts: charging, conservation and quantisation
atomic_skills.description: Describe the two kinds of charge and the force between them; explain charging by friction and the transfer of electrons; apply conservation of charge (sharing of charge between identical spheres) and quantisation of charge using Q = ne.

error_signatures.description: Says protons are transferred during charging by friction
error_signatures.example: Explains a rubbed rod becoming negative by gaining protons

error_signatures.description: Uses the wrong value or sign for the electron charge in Q = ne
error_signatures.example: Takes e as 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C but reports the number of electrons as negative

error_signatures.description: Averages charge incorrectly when two identical spheres touch
error_signatures.example: Adds the charges but forgets to divide by two for identical spheres

error_signatures.description: Says like charges attract
error_signatures.example: Predicts two negatively charged spheres pull together

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Only ELECTRONS move. Gain electrons ⇒ negative; lose electrons ⇒ positive. Like charges repel, unlike attract. Charge is conserved: total before = total after. Two identical spheres that touch SHARE charge equally: each ends with (Q₁+Q₂)/2. Charge is quantised: Q = ne, where e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C and n is a whole number.

levels.title: Electric Circuits
levels.description: EMF, potential difference and current and their measurement; resistance; current and voltage relationships in series and parallel circuits.

atomic_skills.title: Define current, potential difference and EMF and measure them correctly
atomic_skills.description: Define current, potential difference and EMF; describe how an ammeter (in series) and voltmeter (in parallel) are connected; relate the flow of charge to Q = It.

error_signatures.description: Connects an ammeter in parallel and a voltmeter in series
error_signatures.example: Places the ammeter across the resistor and the voltmeter in the main line

error_signatures.description: Defines potential difference as the rate of flow of charge
error_signatures.example: Says potential difference is charge per second

error_signatures.description: Confuses charge, current and time in Q = It
error_signatures.example: Calculates current as Q × t

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Current = rate of flow of charge (Q = It), measured by an AMMETER in SERIES. Potential difference = energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured by a VOLTMETER in PARALLEL (across the component). EMF = the total energy per coulomb supplied by the cell.

atomic_skills.title: Apply current and potential difference rules in series and parallel circuits
atomic_skills.description: Define resistance and use R = V/I; apply the rules that current is the same throughout a series circuit and splits in parallel, while potential difference adds up in series and is the same across parallel branches.

error_signatures.description: Says current splits in series and is equal across parallel branches
error_signatures.example: Divides the current between two resistors in series

error_signatures.description: Adds potential difference across parallel branches
error_signatures.example: Sums the voltages across two parallel resistors

error_signatures.description: Mixes up V, I, R in R = V/I
error_signatures.example: Calculates resistance as I/V

error_signatures.description: Says adding resistors in parallel increases total resistance
error_signatures.example: Predicts total resistance rises when a second parallel resistor is added

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: SERIES: current is the SAME everywhere; potential differences ADD up to the battery voltage. PARALLEL: potential difference is the SAME across each branch; currents ADD up. Resistance R = V/I. Adding resistors in parallel gives more paths ⇒ LOWER total resistance.

levels.title: Classification of Matter
levels.description: Materials and their properties; mixtures (homogeneous/heterogeneous); pure substances, elements and compounds; metals, metalloids and non-metals; conductors, semiconductors and insulators; names and formulae of substances.

atomic_skills.title: Classify matter as mixtures, pure substances, elements, compounds, metals and non-metals
atomic_skills.description: Classify matter as a mixture (homogeneous or heterogeneous) or a pure substance (element or compound); classify substances as metals, metalloids or non-metals and as electrical conductors, semiconductors or insulators, thermal conductors/insulators, and magnetic/non-magnetic using their properties.

error_signatures.description: Classifies a compound as a mixture
error_signatures.example: Calls water a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen

error_signatures.description: Confuses homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures
error_signatures.example: Calls sand-and-water a homogeneous mixture

error_signatures.description: Says metalloids conduct like metals at all temperatures
error_signatures.example: Treats silicon as a normal metallic conductor

error_signatures.description: Treats every shiny element as a metal
error_signatures.example: Classifies graphite as a metal because it conducts

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Matter splits into MIXTURES (physically combined, separable — homogeneous = uniform, heterogeneous = non-uniform) and PURE SUBSTANCES (fixed composition — ELEMENT = one kind of atom, COMPOUND = atoms chemically bonded). Metals conduct and are malleable; non-metals are poor conductors and brittle; metalloids (e.g. Si) are in between and conduct more as temperature rises (semiconductors).

atomic_skills.title: Write and interpret names and formulae of substances
atomic_skills.description: Use the cation and anion tables to write names from formulae and formulae from names; apply the meaning of name endings (-ide, -ite, -ate) and prefixes (mono-, di-, tri-) for ionic and simple covalent compounds.

error_signatures.description: Ignores ion charges when balancing a formula
error_signatures.example: Writes the formula of calcium chloride as CaCl

error_signatures.description: Confuses -ide, -ite and -ate endings
error_signatures.example: Names SO₄²⁻ as sulphite

error_signatures.description: Uses covalent prefixes for an ionic compound
error_signatures.example: Names NaCl as sodium monochloride

error_signatures.description: Forgets brackets around a polyatomic ion taken more than once
error_signatures.example: Writes Ca(NO₃)₂ as CaNO₃₂

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Balance total positive and negative charge to zero (cross the charges as subscripts, e.g. Ca²⁺ + Cl⁻ ⇒ CaCl₂). -ide = simple ion (chloride); -ate = more oxygen (sulphate SO₄²⁻); -ite = less oxygen (sulphite SO₃²⁻). Prefixes (di-, tri-) are for COVALENT compounds (CO₂ = carbon dioxide), not ionic ones. Use brackets for a polyatomic ion used more than once.

levels.title: States of Matter and the Kinetic Molecular Theory
levels.description: The three states of matter, changes of state, melting and boiling points, and the kinetic molecular theory; heating and cooling curves.

tiers.title: States of matter and the kinetic molecular theory

atomic_skills.title: Apply the kinetic molecular theory to states and changes of state
atomic_skills.description: Describe solids, liquids and gases in terms of the kinetic molecular theory (particle arrangement, energy and forces); name the changes of state (melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation, sublimation) and use melting and boiling points to identify the state of a substance at a given temperature; interpret heating and cooling curves.

error_signatures.description: Says temperature rises during a change of state
error_signatures.example: Predicts the temperature keeps climbing while ice is melting

error_signatures.description: Confuses sublimation with evaporation
error_signatures.example: Calls solid-to-gas change evaporation

error_signatures.description: Says particles stop moving in a solid
error_signatures.example: States that solid particles are completely still

error_signatures.description: Reads the wrong state off melting/boiling points
error_signatures.example: Says a substance is liquid at a temperature below its melting point

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: KMT: solids have particles in fixed positions vibrating; liquids' particles are close but move; gases' particles are far apart and fast. Particles ALWAYS move (more energy = faster). During a change of state, temperature stays CONSTANT (energy breaks forces, not raising KE) — these are the flat parts of a heating/cooling curve. Below melting point = solid; between = liquid; above boiling point = gas.

levels.title: The Atom
levels.description: Models of the atom; atomic structure (protons, neutrons, electrons); atomic number, mass number and nuclide notation; isotopes and relative atomic mass; electron configuration.

atomic_skills.title: Apply atomic structure: protons, neutrons, electrons, isotopes and nuclide notation
atomic_skills.description: Use atomic number (Z) and mass number (A) to find the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or ion; write and interpret nuclide notation; define isotopes; calculate relative atomic mass from isotope abundances.

error_signatures.description: Confuses atomic number and mass number
error_signatures.example: Says the number of neutrons equals the atomic number

error_signatures.description: Calculates neutrons as A + Z instead of A − Z
error_signatures.example: Adds atomic number and mass number to get neutrons

error_signatures.description: Says isotopes have different numbers of protons
error_signatures.example: Defines isotopes as atoms with different proton numbers

error_signatures.description: Ignores percentage abundance in the relative atomic mass calculation
error_signatures.example: Takes a simple average of the isotope masses

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Z (atomic number) = protons (= electrons in a neutral atom). A (mass number) = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = A − Z. Isotopes = same element (same Z) but different numbers of neutrons (different A). Relative atomic mass = weighted average = Σ(isotope mass × % abundance)/100.

atomic_skills.title: Write electron configurations (Aufbau, orbital and spectroscopic notation)
atomic_skills.description: Give the electron arrangement of atoms and ions up to Z = 20 using the Aufbau principle, orbital (box) notation and spectroscopic notation (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ …); apply Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle.

error_signatures.description: Fills 3d before 4s, breaking the Aufbau order
error_signatures.example: Writes …3p⁶ 3d² for calcium instead of …3p⁶ 4s²

error_signatures.description: Pairs electrons in one orbital before singly filling degenerate orbitals
error_signatures.example: Pairs both 2p electrons of carbon in the same orbital

error_signatures.description: Miscounts the total electrons against Z
error_signatures.example: Writes a configuration that adds up to 11 electrons for an atom with Z = 12

error_signatures.description: Puts more than two electrons in an orbital
error_signatures.example: Shows three electrons in a single 1s orbital

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Fill in Aufbau order: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d… (4s before 3d). Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons with opposite spins (Pauli). Within a sublevel, place one electron in each orbital before pairing (Hund). The electrons must total Z for a neutral atom.

levels.title: The Periodic Table
levels.description: Position of elements related to electron arrangement; groups and periods; periodicity of atomic radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity; similarities within groups 1, 2, 17 and 18.

atomic_skills.title: Relate position in the periodic table to electron arrangement and periodic trends
atomic_skills.description: Relate an element's group and period to its electron configuration; describe and predict trends across periods and down groups in atomic radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity; relate the chemical similarity of elements in groups 1, 2, 17 and 18 to their valence electrons.

error_signatures.description: Says atomic radius increases across a period (left to right)
error_signatures.example: Predicts chlorine has a larger atomic radius than sodium

error_signatures.description: Says ionisation energy decreases across a period
error_signatures.example: Claims it is easier to remove an electron from neon than from lithium

error_signatures.description: Confuses the trend direction for electronegativity
error_signatures.example: Says electronegativity decreases towards fluorine

error_signatures.description: Relates group number to period instead of valence electrons
error_signatures.example: Says group 2 elements have 2 occupied energy levels

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Group number (1, 2, 17, 18) = number of valence electrons ⇒ similar chemistry within a group. Across a period (→): atomic radius DECREASES, ionisation energy and electronegativity INCREASE (stronger nuclear pull). Down a group (↓): atomic radius INCREASES, ionisation energy and electronegativity DECREASE (more shells, weaker pull).

levels.title: Chemical Bonding
levels.description: Covalent bonding (Lewis diagrams, single/double/triple bonds), ionic bonding (transfer of electrons, ionic lattice) and metallic bonding.

atomic_skills.title: Distinguish covalent, ionic and metallic bonding and draw Lewis diagrams
atomic_skills.description: Define covalent (sharing of electrons), ionic (transfer of electrons forming cations and anions) and metallic (delocalised electrons among positive ions) bonding; draw Lewis/electron diagrams for simple covalent molecules and ions; predict bond type from the elements involved.

error_signatures.description: Says ionic compounds share electrons
error_signatures.example: Describes NaCl as forming a shared pair of electrons

error_signatures.description: Says ionic substances form molecules
error_signatures.example: Refers to a molecule of sodium chloride

error_signatures.description: Draws the wrong number of bonding pairs in a Lewis diagram
error_signatures.example: Shows a single bond in O₂ instead of a double bond

error_signatures.description: Predicts covalent bonding between a metal and a non-metal
error_signatures.example: Says magnesium and oxygen share electrons

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Metal + non-metal ⇒ IONIC (electrons transferred, forming a lattice of ions — no molecules). Non-metal + non-metal ⇒ COVALENT (electrons shared; count pairs to satisfy the octet, e.g. O₂ has a double bond). Metal atoms together ⇒ METALLIC (positive ions in a 'sea' of delocalised electrons). Lewis diagrams show valence electrons as dots/crosses.

levels.title: Physical and Chemical Change
levels.description: Distinguishing physical from chemical change; conservation of atoms and mass; conservation of energy; exothermic and endothermic changes.

atomic_skills.title: Distinguish physical and chemical change and apply conservation laws
atomic_skills.description: Classify a change as physical or chemical from the evidence; apply conservation of atoms and conservation of mass in a reaction; identify changes as exothermic or endothermic and apply conservation of energy.

error_signatures.description: Classifies a change of state as a chemical change
error_signatures.example: Calls melting ice a chemical change

error_signatures.description: Says mass is lost when a gas is produced
error_signatures.example: Claims mass decreases because gas 'disappears' in an open beaker

error_signatures.description: Swaps exothermic and endothermic
error_signatures.example: Calls a reaction that releases heat endothermic

error_signatures.description: Says atoms are created or destroyed in a chemical change
error_signatures.example: Believes new atoms are made when a compound forms

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Physical change: no new substance, easily reversed (e.g. melting, dissolving). Chemical change: new substance forms (colour/gas/precipitate/energy change), hard to reverse. Atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed ⇒ total mass is conserved (account for any gas). Exothermic = RELEASES energy (gets warmer); endothermic = ABSORBS energy (gets colder).

levels.title: Representing Chemical Change
levels.description: Writing and balancing chemical equations with reactants, products and state symbols.

atomic_skills.title: Write and balance chemical equations
atomic_skills.description: Translate a word equation into a balanced chemical equation; balance equations by adjusting coefficients only; include the correct state symbols (s, l, g, aq).

error_signatures.description: Changes a subscript to balance instead of a coefficient
error_signatures.example: Writes H₂O₂ to balance oxygen instead of placing a coefficient

error_signatures.description: Leaves the equation unbalanced
error_signatures.example: Writes H₂ + O₂ → H₂O without balancing

error_signatures.description: Uses the wrong state symbol
error_signatures.example: Labels dissolved sodium chloride as (l) instead of (aq)

error_signatures.description: Forgets diatomic elements exist as molecules
error_signatures.example: Writes O instead of O₂ for oxygen gas

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Balance by changing COEFFICIENTS only — never subscripts. The same number of each atom must appear on both sides. Remember diatomic elements: H₂, O₂, N₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂. State symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.

levels.title: Reactions in Aqueous Solution
levels.description: Ions in aqueous solution and conductivity; ion-exchange reactions — precipitation, gas-forming and acid-base reactions; writing ionic equations.

atomic_skills.title: Identify ions in solution and predict ion-exchange reactions
atomic_skills.description: Relate the conductivity of a solution to the presence of free ions (electrolytes); predict the products of precipitation, gas-forming and acid-base (neutralisation) reactions; write balanced ionic and net ionic equations.

error_signatures.description: Says a sugar solution conducts because it dissolved
error_signatures.example: Predicts a glucose solution conducts electricity

error_signatures.description: Includes spectator ions in a net ionic equation
error_signatures.example: Leaves Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ in the net equation

error_signatures.description: Mislabels a precipitate as soluble
error_signatures.example: Predicts AgCl stays dissolved in solution

error_signatures.description: Forgets that an acid + carbonate releases CO₂ gas
error_signatures.example: Writes an acid-carbonate reaction with no gas product

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Conduction needs FREE IONS — ionic compounds dissolved or molten conduct; molecular solutions (sugar) do not. Ion-exchange: swap the partners. Precipitation = an insoluble solid forms (use solubility rules). Gas-forming = e.g. acid + carbonate ⇒ CO₂. Acid-base = H⁺ + OH⁻ ⇒ H₂O. In a net ionic equation, cancel spectator ions (those unchanged on both sides).

levels.title: Quantitative Aspects of Chemical Change
levels.description: The mole concept — relative atomic and molecular mass, molar mass, the Avogadro number; molar volume of gases, concentration of solutions and stoichiometric calculations.

atomic_skills.title: Apply the mole concept (n = m/M, number of particles, molar mass)
atomic_skills.description: Calculate molar mass from a formula; convert between mass, number of moles and number of particles using n = m/M and N = n × Nₐ; relate relative atomic/molecular mass to molar mass.

error_signatures.description: Inverts n = m/M
error_signatures.example: Calculates moles as molar mass divided by mass

error_signatures.description: Computes molar mass wrong for a compound
error_signatures.example: Gives the molar mass of H₂O as 10 g/mol

error_signatures.description: Uses the wrong Avogadro relationship
error_signatures.example: Divides by Avogadro's number to get particles from moles

error_signatures.description: Ignores subscripts when summing molar mass
error_signatures.example: Adds one O instead of two for CO₂

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Molar mass M = sum of atomic masses (mind the subscripts: CO₂ = 12 + 2×16 = 44 g/mol). Moles n = m/M (mass ÷ molar mass). Number of particles N = n × Nₐ (Nₐ = 6.02×10²³). To go back: n = N/Nₐ.

atomic_skills.title: Apply molar volume, concentration and stoichiometric ratios
atomic_skills.description: Use molar volume of a gas (22.4 dm³ at STP) and concentration c = n/V; use mole ratios from a balanced equation to calculate masses, volumes or amounts of reactants and products.

error_signatures.description: Ignores the mole ratio from the balanced equation
error_signatures.example: Assumes 1:1 moles when the equation gives 1:2

error_signatures.description: Confuses concentration formula c = n/V
error_signatures.example: Calculates concentration as volume divided by moles

error_signatures.description: Mixes up units of volume (cm³ vs dm³)
error_signatures.example: Uses 250 cm³ directly as 250 dm³ in c = n/V

error_signatures.description: Uses molar volume at conditions other than STP
error_signatures.example: Applies 22.4 dm³/mol to a gas not at STP

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Concentration c = n/V (mol/dm³ — convert cm³ to dm³ by ÷1000). At STP, 1 mole of any gas = 22.4 dm³. For reactions: write the balanced equation, convert the known to moles, multiply by the MOLE RATIO from the equation, then convert to the quantity asked for.

levels.title: The Hydrosphere
levels.description: The hydrosphere as a chemical system — water as a resource, ions in water, the interaction of the hydrosphere with other global systems, and threats to water quality.

atomic_skills.title: Describe the hydrosphere, ions in water and threats to water quality
atomic_skills.description: Describe the hydrosphere and its importance as a resource; identify common ions present in natural water and how they get there; describe how the hydrosphere interacts with the atmosphere, lithosphere and biosphere; explain threats to water quality (pollution) and the need to balance water use with conservation.

error_signatures.description: Confuses the hydrosphere with the atmosphere or lithosphere
error_signatures.example: Says the hydrosphere is all the air around Earth

error_signatures.description: Says pure water naturally contains no dissolved ions
error_signatures.example: Claims river water has no dissolved salts

error_signatures.description: Treats fresh water as an unlimited resource
error_signatures.example: Says South Africa has no need to conserve water

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: The hydrosphere = all the water on Earth (oceans, rivers, ice, groundwater, vapour). Natural water dissolves ions from rocks and soil (e.g. Na⁺, Cl⁻, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺), so it is rarely pure. It exchanges matter with the atmosphere, lithosphere and biosphere. Fresh water is a LIMITED resource threatened by pollution (industry, mining, sewage), so use must be balanced with conservation.
